8. Regression Analysis, Gradient & Parameter Extraction

Ordinary least-squares (OLS) linear regression was performed across the six observation pairs. The regression statistics are summarized below:

Slope m = 0.1400 s
Intercept b = Calculated baseline offset
Correlation Coefficient R² = 1.000000
Standard Error of Slope SE_m = ±0.00008 s

9. Uncertainty Propagation & Comparison with Reference

Measurement uncertainty was calculated following the ISO Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM). Type A uncertainty evaluated from observation residuals yielded u_A = 0.0002. Type B instrumental calibration uncertainty from the 6.5-digit multimeter was u_B = 0.0005. The combined expanded uncertainty at a 95% confidence interval (coverage factor k = 2) is:

\[ U = k \cdot \sqrt{u_A^2 + u_B^2} = 2 \cdot \sqrt{(0.0002)^2 + (0.0005)^2} = \pm 0.0011\text{ s} \]

The experimental estimate of 0.14 s agrees with the theoretical reference value (0.14 s) within an absolute deviation of 0.015%, well within the expanded uncertainty band.

10. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretations

The experimental results confirm the theoretical behavior of idmt protective relays. The linearity observed across all six test points validates the assumption of linear, bilateral network characteristics. Thermal drift was effectively suppressed by maintaining low duty cycles and utilizing precision metal-film components. The minor residual fluctuations observed are attributable to quantization resolution and Johnson–Nyquist thermal noise in the passive bridge elements.

11. Industrial Applications & Construction Practice

The electrotechnical principles demonstrated in this laboratory form the core foundation of numerous modern engineering systems, including:

  • Power Grid & Transmission Engineering: Network equivalent modeling, short-circuit current calculations, power factor correction capacitor banks, and substation protective relay coordination.
  • Consumer Electronics & Integrated Circuits: Analog front-end amplification, active Butterworth filtering, switching power supply voltage regulation, and precision ADC/DAC mixed-signal conversion.
  • Industrial Automation & Drives: Variable frequency motor speed control, servomechanism closed-loop feedback, electromechanical energy conversion, and industrial PLC signal conditioning.

12. Conclusion & Recommendations

The experimental investigation of Inverse Definite Minimum Time (IDMT) Overcurrent and Earth-Fault Relay Characteristics was completed with complete success. The linear regression model verified the governing transfer equation with R² = 1.000000. All experimental safety protocols and precision measurement guidelines were strictly observed. For future investigations, automated GPIB/USB telemetry acquisition and environmental temperature chamber testing are recommended to characterize high-temperature coefficients.

Simulated demonstration data.

This report presents simulated benchmark observations generated for demonstration and academic instruction purposes. When submitting coursework, replace all numerical values with your actual laboratory workbench observations.

1. Theoretical Principles of Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Module IV/PV Characteristics & Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT)

Electrical and Electronics Engineering rests upon Maxwell's field equations, Ohm's empirical law of conduction, and Kirchhoff's conservation laws for current (KCL) and voltage (KVL). In this laboratory investigation of Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Module IV/PV Characteristics & Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT), we examine the fundamental electrotechnical relationships within the solar simulator & electronic load mppt controller. The core focus of this module addresses photon absorption, carrier recombination, single-diode model & temperature de-rating.

Under steady-state excitation, the physical system conforms to the governing linear transfer characteristic:

\[ y = m \cdot x + b \]

where $x$ represents the normalized independent input variable (Incident Solar Irradiance G, in units of $W/m²$), $y$ denotes the measured response variable (Short-Circuit Photocurrent I_sc, in units of $A$), $m$ represents the characteristic transfer gradient ($0.00485$), and $b$ accounts for the intrinsic offset or baseline bias.

2. Mathematical Derivations & Network Formulations

Consider the canonical lumped-parameter circuit model representing the device under test. Applying Kirchhoff's voltage law around the primary loop yields:

\[ \sum_{k=1}^{N} V_k = 0 \implies V_{source} - I \cdot R_{int} - V_{term} = 0 \]

Rearranging in terms of measurable terminal telemetry provides the explicit affine calibration equation:

\[ I_sc = 0.00485 · G \]

The derivative $\frac{dy}{dx} = m = 0.00485$ represents the fundamental sensitivity coefficient (Photovoltaic Current Responsivity (I_sc/G)). For active linear networks, this slope characterizes internal Thévenin/Norton source impedances, transconductance gains, resonance quality factors, or machine electromechanical couplings depending on the specific circuit topology.

3. Dynamic Behavior, Energy Storage & Frequency Dependencies

In circuits containing reactive elements (inductors $L$ and capacitors $C$), the instantaneous terminal dynamics obey differential operator equations:

\[ v_L(t) = L \frac{di(t)}{dt}, \quad i_C(t) = C \frac{dv_C(t)}{dt} \]

Under sinusoidal steady-state AC conditions, time-domain derivatives map directly to the complex frequency domain via the Laplace transform $s = j\omega = j 2\pi f$. The total complex impedance $\mathbf{Z}(j\omega)$ combines real resistive dissipation $R$ with quadrature reactive energy storage $X(\omega) = \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}$:

\[ \mathbf{Z}(j\omega) = R + j \left( \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} \right) = |Z| e^{j\phi} \]

Phase angle $\phi = \arctan\left(\frac{X}{R}\right)$ dictates power factor ($\cos\phi$), defining the balance between real work-producing power $P = V I \cos\phi$ and circulating reactive power $Q = V I \sin\phi$.

4. Semiconductor Physics & Operational Boundary Limits

When active solid-state semiconductors or magnetic cores are present in the subsystem, small-signal linearity holds strictly within small-signal perturbation bounds. For semiconductor junctions, minority carrier diffusion and space-charge recombination follow Shockley's exponential law $I = I_s (e^{V / \eta V_T} - 1)$. For ferromagnetic inductors and transformer cores, magnetic flux density $B$ relates to magnetic field intensity $H$ through the non-linear hysteresis loop $B = \mu(H) H$, reaching magnetic saturation at high flux densities. Standard laboratory operating points are deliberately biased within the linear, unsaturated small-signal domain to guarantee high parameter reproducibility and minimal harmonic distortion.

5. Instrumentation Architecture & Error Minimization

To eliminate systematic measurement offsets, modern electrical metrology incorporates digital signal processing (DSP) filters, high-input-impedance JFET-input instrumentation amplifiers ($Z_{in} > 10^{12}\,\Omega$), and true-RMS AC conversion algorithms. The calibrated measurement protocol utilizes four-terminal Kelvin connections to isolate lead resistance drops, while high-frequency coaxial lines are terminated in their characteristic impedance ($50\,\Omega$) to suppress transmission line standing wave reflections.

2. Abstract

An experimental investigation of wind turbine power curve was conducted using precision laboratory instrumentation across six systematic setpoints of velocity cubed v³ ranging from 125.0 to 1000.0 (m/s)³. Measured generator output power p_e data were logged using 6.5-digit digital multimeters and digital storage oscilloscopes. Ordinary least-squares regression yielded an empirical calibration line of P_e = 0.4200 · v³ with a coefficient of determination R² = 1.000000.   • Calibrated Decade Resistance & Component Substitution Box: Provides precision 0.1% tolerance standard passive values to establish calibrated velocity cubed v³ conditions.

4. Theory & Graphical Coordinate Selection

According to the principles of wind turbine power curve, the circuit response follows the linear transformation:

P_e = 0.4200 · v³

\[ V_peak = 45.0000 · N \]

theory:
1. Theoretical Principles of Power Quality Analysis: Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) and FFT Spectral Harmonics

Electrical and Electronics Engineering rests upon Maxwell's field equations, Ohm's empirical law of conduction, and Kirchhoff's conservation laws for current (KCL) and voltage (KVL). In this laboratory investigation of Power Quality Analysis: Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) and FFT Spectral Harmonics, we examine the fundamental electrotechnical relationships within the power quality analyzer & controllable thyristor bridge. The core focus of this module addresses fourier decomposition, non-linear load harmonics, ieee 519 compliance & active filtering.

Under steady-state excitation, the physical system conforms to the governing linear transfer characteristic:

\[ y = m \cdot x + b \]

where $x$ represents the normalized independent input variable (Thyristor Firing Angle Delay α, in units of $deg$), $y$ denotes the measured response variable (Current Total Harmonic Distortion THD_I, in units of $%$), $m$ represents the characteristic transfer gradient ($0.5500$), and $b$ accounts for the intrinsic offset or baseline bias.

2. Mathematical Derivations & Network Formulations

Consider the canonical lumped-parameter circuit model representing the device under test. Applying Kirchhoff's voltage law around the primary loop yields:

\[ \sum_{k=1}^{N} V_k = 0 \implies V_{source} - I \cdot R_{int} - V_{term} = 0 \]

Rearranging in terms of measurable terminal telemetry provides the explicit affine calibration equation:

\[ THD_I = 0.5500 · α + 12.0000 \]

The derivative $\frac{dy}{dx} = m = 0.5500$ represents the fundamental sensitivity coefficient (Harmonic Distortion Angular Sensitivity Slope). For active linear networks, this slope characterizes internal Thévenin/Norton source impedances, transconductance gains, resonance quality factors, or machine electromechanical couplings depending on the specific circuit topology.

3. Dynamic Behavior, Energy Storage & Frequency Dependencies

In circuits containing reactive elements (inductors $L$ and capacitors $C$), the instantaneous terminal dynamics obey differential operator equations:

\[ v_L(t) = L \frac{di(t)}{dt}, \quad i_C(t) = C \frac{dv_C(t)}{dt} \]

Under sinusoidal steady-state AC conditions, time-domain derivatives map directly to the complex frequency domain via the Laplace transform $s = j\omega = j 2\pi f$. The total complex impedance $\mathbf{Z}(j\omega)$ combines real resistive dissipation $R$ with quadrature reactive energy storage $X(\omega) = \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}$:

\[ \mathbf{Z}(j\omega) = R + j \left( \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} \right) = |Z| e^{j\phi} \]

Phase angle $\phi = \arctan\left(\frac{X}{R}\right)$ dictates power factor ($\cos\phi$), defining the balance between real work-producing power $P = V I \cos\phi$ and circulating reactive power $Q = V I \sin\phi$.

4. Semiconductor Physics & Operational Boundary Limits

When active solid-state semiconductors or magnetic cores are present in the subsystem, small-signal linearity holds strictly within small-signal perturbation bounds. For semiconductor junctions, minority carrier diffusion and space-charge recombination follow Shockley's exponential law $I = I_s (e^{V / \eta V_T} - 1)$. For ferromagnetic inductors and transformer cores, magnetic flux density $B$ relates to magnetic field intensity $H$ through the non-linear hysteresis loop $B = \mu(H) H$, reaching magnetic saturation at high flux densities. Standard laboratory operating points are deliberately biased within the linear, unsaturated small-signal domain to guarantee high parameter reproducibility and minimal harmonic distortion.

5. Instrumentation Architecture & Error Minimization

To eliminate systematic measurement offsets, modern electrical metrology incorporates digital signal processing (DSP) filters, high-input-impedance JFET-input instrumentation amplifiers ($Z_{in} > 10^{12}\,\Omega$), and true-RMS AC conversion algorithms. The calibrated measurement protocol utilizes four-terminal Kelvin connections to isolate lead resistance drops, while high-frequency coaxial lines are terminated in their characteristic impedance ($50\,\Omega$) to suppress transmission line standing wave reflections.
report:
1. Title and Objective

Power Quality Analysis: Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) and FFT Spectral Harmonics. Measure Total Harmonic Distortion (THD_V and THD_I), individual harmonic amplitudes, and distortion power factor generated by non-linear phase-controlled rectifier loads. This formal laboratory report documents experimental data acquisition, mathematical model calibration, regression analysis, and error propagation for power quality & thd.

2. Abstract

An experimental investigation of power quality & thd was conducted using precision laboratory instrumentation across six systematic setpoints of firing angle α ranging from 15.0 to 65.0 deg. Measured current total harmonic distortion thd_i data were logged using 6.5-digit digital multimeters and digital storage oscilloscopes. Ordinary least-squares regression yielded an empirical calibration line of THD_I = 0.5500 · α + 12.0000 with a coefficient of determination R² = 1.000000. The derived experimental parameter Harmonic Distortion Angular Sensitivity Slope was evaluated as 0.55 %/deg, demonstrating complete agreement with theoretical benchmark expectations within 0.02% experimental error.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Standard Settings

  • Power Quality & THD Precision Workstation: Provides regulated excitation, calibrated terminal access, and low-parasitic interconnects for fourier decomposition, non-linear load harmonics, ieee 519 compliance & active filtering.
  • True-RMS Digital Multimeter (6.5-digit Keysight / Fluke): Measures terminal voltages, branch currents, and precision DC/AC parameters with ±0.0035% baseline accuracy.
  • Dual-Channel Digital Storage Oscilloscope (100 MHz, 1 GSa/s): Captures time-domain waveforms, phase shifts, transient dynamics, and harmonic spectra for power quality & thd.
  • Regulated Linear DC / AC Variable Power Source: Supplies low-noise, ripple-free voltage and current excitation with adjustable current limiting.
  • Calibrated Decade Resistance & Component Substitution Box: Provides precision 0.1% tolerance standard passive values to establish calibrated firing angle α conditions.
  • Four-Terminal Kelvin Lead Wire & BNC Coaxial Cable Set: Minimizes lead resistance, inductive pickup, and ambient EMI interference across all test ports.
  • Environmental Ambient Conditions: Ambient laboratory temperature 23.5 ± 0.5 °C; relative humidity 45 ± 5%; atmospheric pressure 101.3 kPa.
  • Excitation Calibration Settings: Primary source stabilized within ±0.01% using closed-loop linear voltage regulation.

4. Theory & Graphical Coordinate Selection

According to the principles of power quality & thd, the circuit response follows the linear transformation:

THD_I = 0.5500 · α + 12.0000

To evaluate the intrinsic physical parameter (Harmonic Distortion Angular Sensitivity Slope), the experimental data are plotted with Firing angle delay α (deg) on the horizontal abscissa and Current total harmonic distortion THD_I (%) on the vertical ordinate. The gradient of the resulting least-squares linear line directly yields the parameter magnitude.

5. Step-by-Step Experimental Method

  1. Visual Inspection & Pre-Flight Zero Tare: Inspect all circuit connections, breadboard jumpers, and terminal blocks. Verify that instrument ground planes are tied to earth and execute zero tare on all digital meters.
  2. Excitation Source & Baseline Calibration: Energize the regulated supply, set baseline operating thresholds, and calibrate the firing angle α using the precision standard reference meter.
  3. Systematic Parameter Variation & Settling: Increment the firing angle α systematically across the designated experimental range (15.0 to 65.0 deg), permitting thermal settling at each setpoint.
  4. Multi-Meter & Oscilloscope Waveform Acquisition: Record the primary output metric (Current Total Harmonic Distortion THD_I) alongside auxiliary telemetry. Verify waveform symmetry, DC offset, and harmonic integrity on the oscilloscope.
  5. Cross-Validation & Redundant Trial Verification: Execute repeated forward and reverse sweeps to detect hysteresis, thermal drift, or non-linear saturation effects across the device under test (DUT).
  6. Shutdown, De-energization & Data Archival: Reduce source excitation smoothly to zero, de-energize all primary supplies, discharge residual capacitive elements, and export raw telemetry to the data buffer.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Data Tabulation

All experimental observations were recorded under steady-state thermal and electrical equilibrium. The table below summarizes the recorded telemetry across the experimental domain.

Table 1. Experimental observation telemetry for Power Quality & THD.
Trial # Thyristor Firing Angle Delay α (deg) Current Total Harmonic Distortion THD_I (%) Transformed x Transformed y Residual

225.013.7525.00013.7500.000
335.019.2535.00019.2500.000
445.024.7545.00024.7500.000
555.030.2555.00030.2500.000
665.035.7565.00035.7500.000

7. Worked Calculation for Representative Observation

For Trial 3 (Firing Angle α = 35.0 deg):

x_3 = 35.0 deg
y_3 = m \cdot x_3 + b = THD_I = 0.5500 · α + 12.0000
Derived Parameter Value = 0.55 %/deg

8. Regression Analysis, Gradient & Parameter Extraction

Ordinary least-squares (OLS) linear regression was performed across the six observation pairs. The regression statistics are summarized below:

Slope m = 0.5500 %/deg
Intercept b = Calculated baseline offset
Correlation Coefficient R² = 1.000000
Standard Error of Slope SE_m = ±0.00008 %/deg

9. Uncertainty Propagation & Comparison with Reference

Measurement uncertainty was calculated following the ISO Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM). Type A uncertainty evaluated from observation residuals yielded u_A = 0.0002. Type B instrumental calibration uncertainty from the 6.5-digit multimeter was u_B = 0.0005. The combined expanded uncertainty at a 95% confidence interval (coverage factor k = 2) is:

\[ U = k \cdot \sqrt{u_A^2 + u_B^2} = 2 \cdot \sqrt{(0.0002)^2 + (0.0005)^2} = \pm 0.0011\text{ %/deg} \]

The experimental estimate of 0.55 %/deg agrees with the theoretical reference value (0.55 %/deg) within an absolute deviation of 0.015%, well within the expanded uncertainty band.

10. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretations

The experimental results confirm the theoretical behavior of power quality & thd. The linearity observed across all six test points validates the assumption of linear, bilateral network characteristics. Thermal drift was effectively suppressed by maintaining low duty cycles and utilizing precision metal-film components. The minor residual fluctuations observed are attributable to quantization resolution and Johnson–Nyquist thermal noise in the passive bridge elements.

11. Industrial Applications & Construction Practice

The electrotechnical principles demonstrated in this laboratory form the core foundation of numerous modern engineering systems, including:

  • Power Grid & Transmission Engineering: Network equivalent modeling, short-circuit current calculations, power factor correction capacitor banks, and substation protective relay coordination.
  • Consumer Electronics & Integrated Circuits: Analog front-end amplification, active Butterworth filtering, switching power supply voltage regulation, and precision ADC/DAC mixed-signal conversion.
  • Industrial Automation & Drives: Variable frequency motor speed control, servomechanism closed-loop feedback, electromechanical energy conversion, and industrial PLC signal conditioning.

12. Conclusion & Recommendations

The experimental investigation of Power Quality Analysis: Total Harmonic Distortion (THD) and FFT Spectral Harmonics was completed with complete success. The linear regression model verified the governing transfer equation with R² = 1.000000. All experimental safety protocols and precision measurement guidelines were strictly observed. For future investigations, automated GPIB/USB telemetry acquisition and environmental temperature chamber testing are recommended to characterize high-temperature coefficients.

This report presents simulated benchmark observations generated for demonstration and academic instruction purposes. When submitting coursework, replace all numerical values with your actual laboratory workbench observations.

topics.question: How does varying Firing Factor affect the circuit response?
topics.answer: Changing Firing Factor shifts the operating point along the characteristic transfer function, modulating internal voltage drops and current distributions as governed by V_dc = 48.0000 · (1 + cos α).

topics.question: Why is impedance matching essential in high-frequency and power systems?
topics.answer: Impedance matching eliminates reflected wave power in transmission networks and maximizes energy transfer efficiency from source to load according to the Maximum Power Transfer Theorem.

topics.question: How do non-linear parasitic components introduce measurement error in this lab?
topics.answer: Parasitic lead inductances, stray capacitances, and temperature-dependent resistance shifts introduce high-frequency distortion and baseline drift if not compensated by Kelvin four-wire sensing.

topics.question: What distinguishes the analytical model from experimental observations in SCR & TRIAC Firing Control?
topics.answer: Ideal analytical formulas assume zero internal dissipation and infinite bandwidth, whereas real physical components exhibit finite dielectric losses, saturation limits, and ambient thermal sensitivity.

topics.question: How are these electrical principles applied in modern microelectronics and grid infrastructure?
topics.answer: The concepts form the backbone of power electronics converters, integrated circuit biasing, smart grid protection relays, renewable energy inverters, and high-speed communication transceivers.

theory:
1. Theoretical Principles of High-Efficiency DC-DC Step-Down (Buck) and Step-Up (Boost) Switched-Mode Power Converters

Electrical and Electronics Engineering rests upon Maxwell's field equations, Ohm's empirical law of conduction, and Kirchhoff's conservation laws for current (KCL) and voltage (KVL). In this laboratory investigation of High-Efficiency DC-DC Step-Down (Buck) and Step-Up (Boost) Switched-Mode Power Converters, we examine the fundamental electrotechnical relationships within the 100-khz switched-mode power supply (smps) breadboard. The core focus of this module addresses continuous vs discontinuous conduction modes (ccm/dcm), inductor volt-second balance.

Under steady-state excitation, the physical system conforms to the governing linear transfer characteristic:

\[ y = m \cdot x + b \]

where $x$ represents the normalized independent input variable (Switched PWM Duty Ratio D, in units of $ratio$), $y$ denotes the measured response variable (Step-Down Output Voltage V_out, in units of $V$), $m$ represents the characteristic transfer gradient ($24.0000$), and $b$ accounts for the intrinsic offset or baseline bias.

2. Mathematical Derivations & Network Formulations

Consider the canonical lumped-parameter circuit model representing the device under test. Applying Kirchhoff's voltage law around the primary loop yields:

\[ \sum_{k=1}^{N} V_k = 0 \implies V_{source} - I \cdot R_{int} - V_{term} = 0 \]

Rearranging in terms of measurable terminal telemetry provides the explicit affine calibration equation:

\[ V_out = 24.0000 · D \]

The derivative $\frac{dy}{dx} = m = 24.0000$ represents the fundamental sensitivity coefficient (Buck Converter Input Voltage Scaling (V_in)). For active linear networks, this slope characterizes internal Thévenin/Norton source impedances, transconductance gains, resonance quality factors, or machine electromechanical couplings depending on the specific circuit topology.

3. Dynamic Behavior, Energy Storage & Frequency Dependencies

In circuits containing reactive elements (inductors $L$ and capacitors $C$), the instantaneous terminal dynamics obey differential operator equations:

\[ v_L(t) = L \frac{di(t)}{dt}, \quad i_C(t) = C \frac{dv_C(t)}{dt} \]

Under sinusoidal steady-state AC conditions, time-domain derivatives map directly to the complex frequency domain via the Laplace transform $s = j\omega = j 2\pi f$. The total complex impedance $\mathbf{Z}(j\omega)$ combines real resistive dissipation $R$ with quadrature reactive energy storage $X(\omega) = \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}$:

\[ \mathbf{Z}(j\omega) = R + j \left( \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} \right) = |Z| e^{j\phi} \]

Phase angle $\phi = \arctan\left(\frac{X}{R}\right)$ dictates power factor ($\cos\phi$), defining the balance between real work-producing power $P = V I \cos\phi$ and circulating reactive power $Q = V I \sin\phi$.

4. Semiconductor Physics & Operational Boundary Limits

When active solid-state semiconductors or magnetic cores are present in the subsystem, small-signal linearity holds strictly within small-signal perturbation bounds. For semiconductor junctions, minority carrier diffusion and space-charge recombination follow Shockley's exponential law $I = I_s (e^{V / \eta V_T} - 1)$. For ferromagnetic inductors and transformer cores, magnetic flux density $B$ relates to magnetic field intensity $H$ through the non-linear hysteresis loop $B = \mu(H) H$, reaching magnetic saturation at high flux densities. Standard laboratory operating points are deliberately biased within the linear, unsaturated small-signal domain to guarantee high parameter reproducibility and minimal harmonic distortion.

5. Instrumentation Architecture & Error Minimization

To eliminate systematic measurement offsets, modern electrical metrology incorporates digital signal processing (DSP) filters, high-input-impedance JFET-input instrumentation amplifiers ($Z_{in} > 10^{12}\,\Omega$), and true-RMS AC conversion algorithms. The calibrated measurement protocol utilizes four-terminal Kelvin connections to isolate lead resistance drops, while high-frequency coaxial lines are terminated in their characteristic impedance ($50\,\Omega$) to suppress transmission line standing wave reflections.
report:
1. Title and Objective

High-Efficiency DC-DC Step-Down (Buck) and Step-Up (Boost) Switched-Mode Power Converters. Design, assemble, and test a high-frequency MOSFET-switched buck converter, determining output voltage transfer ratio (V_out = D·V_in), inductor current ripple, and conversion efficiency. This formal laboratory report documents experimental data acquisition, mathematical model calibration, regression analysis, and error propagation for buck-boost dc-dc converters.

2. Abstract

An experimental investigation of buck-boost dc-dc converters was conducted using precision laboratory instrumentation across six systematic setpoints of duty ratio d ranging from 0.15 to 0.8 ratio. Measured step-down output voltage v_out data were logged using 6.5-digit digital multimeters and digital storage oscilloscopes. Ordinary least-squares regression yielded an empirical calibration line of V_out = 24.0000 · D with a coefficient of determination R² = 1.000000. The derived experimental parameter Buck Converter Input Voltage Scaling (V_in) was evaluated as 24.0 V, demonstrating complete agreement with theoretical benchmark expectations within 0.02% experimental error.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Standard Settings

  • Buck-Boost DC-DC Converters Precision Workstation: Provides regulated excitation, calibrated terminal access, and low-parasitic interconnects for continuous vs discontinuous conduction modes (ccm/dcm), inductor volt-second balance.
  • True-RMS Digital Multimeter (6.5-digit Keysight / Fluke): Measures terminal voltages, branch currents, and precision DC/AC parameters with ±0.0035% baseline accuracy.
  • Dual-Channel Digital Storage Oscilloscope (100 MHz, 1 GSa/s): Captures time-domain waveforms, phase shifts, transient dynamics, and harmonic spectra for buck-boost dc-dc converters.
  • Regulated Linear DC / AC Variable Power Source: Supplies low-noise, ripple-free voltage and current excitation with adjustable current limiting.
  • Calibrated Decade Resistance & Component Substitution Box: Provides precision 0.1% tolerance standard passive values to establish calibrated duty ratio d conditions.
  • Four-Terminal Kelvin Lead Wire & BNC Coaxial Cable Set: Minimizes lead resistance, inductive pickup, and ambient EMI interference across all test ports.
  • Environmental Ambient Conditions: Ambient laboratory temperature 23.5 ± 0.5 °C; relative humidity 45 ± 5%; atmospheric pressure 101.3 kPa.
  • Excitation Calibration Settings: Primary source stabilized within ±0.01% using closed-loop linear voltage regulation.

4. Theory & Graphical Coordinate Selection

According to the principles of buck-boost dc-dc converters, the circuit response follows the linear transformation:

V_out = 24.0000 · D

To evaluate the intrinsic physical parameter (Buck Converter Input Voltage Scaling (V_in)), the experimental data are plotted with PWM duty ratio D (ratio) on the horizontal abscissa and Step-down output voltage V_out (V) on the vertical ordinate. The gradient of the resulting least-squares linear line directly yields the parameter magnitude.

5. Step-by-Step Experimental Method

  1. Visual Inspection & Pre-Flight Zero Tare: Inspect all circuit connections, breadboard jumpers, and terminal blocks. Verify that instrument ground planes are tied to earth and execute zero tare on all digital meters.
  2. Excitation Source & Baseline Calibration: Energize the regulated supply, set baseline operating thresholds, and calibrate the duty ratio d using the precision standard reference meter.
  3. Systematic Parameter Variation & Settling: Increment the duty ratio d systematically across the designated experimental range (0.15 to 0.8 ratio), permitting thermal settling at each setpoint.
  4. Multi-Meter & Oscilloscope Waveform Acquisition: Record the primary output metric (Step-Down Output Voltage V_out) alongside auxiliary telemetry. Verify waveform symmetry, DC offset, and harmonic integrity on the oscilloscope.
  5. Cross-Validation & Redundant Trial Verification: Execute repeated forward and reverse sweeps to detect hysteresis, thermal drift, or non-linear saturation effects across the device under test (DUT).
  6. Shutdown, De-energization & Data Archival: Reduce source excitation smoothly to zero, de-energize all primary supplies, discharge residual capacitive elements, and export raw telemetry to the data buffer.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Data Tabulation

All experimental observations were recorded under steady-state thermal and electrical equilibrium. The table below summarizes the recorded telemetry across the experimental domain.

7. Worked Calculation for Representative Observation

For Trial 3 (Duty Ratio D = 0.42 ratio):

x_3 = 0.42 ratio
y_3 = m \cdot x_3 + b = V_ou0.42 = 24.0000 · D
Derived Parameter Value = 24.0 V

8. Regression Analysis, Gradient & Parameter Extraction

Ordinary least-squares (OLS) linear regression was performed across the six observation pairs. The regression statistics are summarized below:

Slope m = 24.0000 V
Intercept b = Calculated baseline offset
Correlation Coefficient R² = 1.000000
Standard Error of Slope SE_m = ±0.00008 V

9. Uncertainty Propagation & Comparison with Reference

Measurement uncertainty was calculated following the ISO Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM). Type A uncertainty evaluated from observation residuals yielded u_A = 0.0002. Type B instrumental calibration uncertainty from the 6.5-digit multimeter was u_B = 0.0005. The combined expanded uncertainty at a 95% confidence interval (coverage factor k = 2) is:

\[ U = k \cdot \sqrt{u_A^2 + u_B^2} = 2 \cdot \sqrt{(0.0002)^2 + (0.0005)^2} = \pm 0.0011\text{ V} \]

The experimental estimate of 24.0 V agrees with the theoretical reference value (24.0 V) within an absolute deviation of 0.015%, well within the expanded uncertainty band.

10. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretations

The experimental results confirm the theoretical behavior of buck-boost dc-dc converters. The linearity observed across all six test points validates the assumption of linear, bilateral network characteristics. Thermal drift was effectively suppressed by maintaining low duty cycles and utilizing precision metal-film components. The minor residual fluctuations observed are attributable to quantization resolution and Johnson–Nyquist thermal noise in the passive bridge elements.

11. Industrial Applications & Construction Practice

The electrotechnical principles demonstrated in this laboratory form the core foundation of numerous modern engineering systems, including:

  • Power Grid & Transmission Engineering: Network equivalent modeling, short-circuit current calculations, power factor correction capacitor banks, and substation protective relay coordination.
  • Consumer Electronics & Integrated Circuits: Analog front-end amplification, active Butterworth filtering, switching power supply voltage regulation, and precision ADC/DAC mixed-signal conversion.
  • Industrial Automation & Drives: Variable frequency motor speed control, servomechanism closed-loop feedback, electromechanical energy conversion, and industrial PLC signal conditioning.

12. Conclusion & Recommendations

The experimental investigation of High-Efficiency DC-DC Step-Down (Buck) and Step-Up (Boost) Switched-Mode Power Converters was completed with complete success. The linear regression model verified the governing transfer equation with R² = 1.000000. All experimental safety protocols and precision measurement guidelines were strictly observed. For future investigations, automated GPIB/USB telemetry acquisition and environmental temperature chamber testing are recommended to characterize high-temperature coefficients.

Simulated demonstration data.

This report presents simulated benchmark observations generated for demonstration and academic instruction purposes. When submitting coursework, replace all numerical values with your actual laboratory workbench observations.

theory:
1. Theoretical Principles of Closed-Loop Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) DC Motor Speed Servomechanism

Electrical and Electronics Engineering rests upon Maxwell's field equations, Ohm's empirical law of conduction, and Kirchhoff's conservation laws for current (KCL) and voltage (KVL). In this laboratory investigation of Closed-Loop Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) DC Motor Speed Servomechanism, we examine the fundamental electrotechnical relationships within the analog pid controller board & optical quadrature encoder servomotor. The core focus of this module addresses root locus dynamics, ziegler-nichols tuning, integral windup & phase margin.

Under steady-state excitation, the physical system conforms to the governing linear transfer characteristic:

\[ y = m \cdot x + b \]

where $x$ represents the normalized independent input variable (Controller Proportional Gain K_p, in units of $gain$), $y$ denotes the measured response variable (Closed-Loop Natural Angular Frequency ω_n, in units of $rad/s$), $m$ represents the characteristic transfer gradient ($5.2000$), and $b$ accounts for the intrinsic offset or baseline bias.

2. Mathematical Derivations & Network Formulations

Consider the canonical lumped-parameter circuit model representing the device under test. Applying Kirchhoff's voltage law around the primary loop yields:

\[ \sum_{k=1}^{N} V_k = 0 \implies V_{source} - I \cdot R_{int} - V_{term} = 0 \]

Rearranging in terms of measurable terminal telemetry provides the explicit affine calibration equation:

\[ ω_n = 5.2000 · K_p + 10.0000 \]

The derivative $\frac{dy}{dx} = m = 5.2000$ represents the fundamental sensitivity coefficient (Closed-Loop Bandwidth Scaling Gradient). For active linear networks, this slope characterizes internal Thévenin/Norton source impedances, transconductance gains, resonance quality factors, or machine electromechanical couplings depending on the specific circuit topology.

3. Dynamic Behavior, Energy Storage & Frequency Dependencies

In circuits containing reactive elements (inductors $L$ and capacitors $C$), the instantaneous terminal dynamics obey differential operator equations:

\[ v_L(t) = L \frac{di(t)}{dt}, \quad i_C(t) = C \frac{dv_C(t)}{dt} \]

Under sinusoidal steady-state AC conditions, time-domain derivatives map directly to the complex frequency domain via the Laplace transform $s = j\omega = j 2\pi f$. The total complex impedance $\mathbf{Z}(j\omega)$ combines real resistive dissipation $R$ with quadrature reactive energy storage $X(\omega) = \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}$:

\[ \mathbf{Z}(j\omega) = R + j \left( \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} \right) = |Z| e^{j\phi} \]

Phase angle $\phi = \arctan\left(\frac{X}{R}\right)$ dictates power factor ($\cos\phi$), defining the balance between real work-producing power $P = V I \cos\phi$ and circulating reactive power $Q = V I \sin\phi$.

4. Semiconductor Physics & Operational Boundary Limits

When active solid-state semiconductors or magnetic cores are present in the subsystem, small-signal linearity holds strictly within small-signal perturbation bounds. For semiconductor junctions, minority carrier diffusion and space-charge recombination follow Shockley's exponential law $I = I_s (e^{V / \eta V_T} - 1)$. For ferromagnetic inductors and transformer cores, magnetic flux density $B$ relates to magnetic field intensity $H$ through the non-linear hysteresis loop $B = \mu(H) H$, reaching magnetic saturation at high flux densities. Standard laboratory operating points are deliberately biased within the linear, unsaturated small-signal domain to guarantee high parameter reproducibility and minimal harmonic distortion.

5. Instrumentation Architecture & Error Minimization

To eliminate systematic measurement offsets, modern electrical metrology incorporates digital signal processing (DSP) filters, high-input-impedance JFET-input instrumentation amplifiers ($Z_{in} > 10^{12}\,\Omega$), and true-RMS AC conversion algorithms. The calibrated measurement protocol utilizes four-terminal Kelvin connections to isolate lead resistance drops, while high-frequency coaxial lines are terminated in their characteristic impedance ($50\,\Omega$) to suppress transmission line standing wave reflections.

1. Theoretical Principles of Piezoresistive Foil Strain Gauge and Temperature-Compensated Wheatstone Bridge Circuitry

Electrical and Electronics Engineering rests upon Maxwell's field equations, Ohm's empirical law of conduction, and Kirchhoff's conservation laws for current (KCL) and voltage (KVL). In this laboratory investigation of Piezoresistive Foil Strain Gauge and Temperature-Compensated Wheatstone Bridge Circuitry, we examine the fundamental electrotechnical relationships within the precision cantilever bending rig & instrumentation amplifier. The core focus of this module addresses piezoresistive strain effect, dummy gauge thermal compensation & full-bridge gain.

Under steady-state excitation, the physical system conforms to the governing linear transfer characteristic:

\[ y = m \cdot x + b \]

where $x$ represents the normalized independent input variable (Applied Mechanical Microstrain με, in units of $με$), $y$ denotes the measured response variable (Bridge Differential Output Voltage V_out, in units of $mV$), $m$ represents the characteristic transfer gradient ($0.0125$), and $b$ accounts for the intrinsic offset or baseline bias.

2. Mathematical Derivations & Network Formulations

Consider the canonical lumped-parameter circuit model representing the device under test. Applying Kirchhoff's voltage law around the primary loop yields:

\[ \sum_{k=1}^{N} V_k = 0 \implies V_{source} - I \cdot R_{int} - V_{term} = 0 \]

Rearranging in terms of measurable terminal telemetry provides the explicit affine calibration equation:

\[ V_out = 0.0125 · με \]

The derivative $\frac{dy}{dx} = m = 0.0125$ represents the fundamental sensitivity coefficient (Full-Bridge Strain Sensitivity Factor (GF·V_ex/4)). For active linear networks, this slope characterizes internal Thévenin/Norton source impedances, transconductance gains, resonance quality factors, or machine electromechanical couplings depending on the specific circuit topology.

3. Dynamic Behavior, Energy Storage & Frequency Dependencies

In circuits containing reactive elements (inductors $L$ and capacitors $C$), the instantaneous terminal dynamics obey differential operator equations:

\[ v_L(t) = L \frac{di(t)}{dt}, \quad i_C(t) = C \frac{dv_C(t)}{dt} \]

Under sinusoidal steady-state AC conditions, time-domain derivatives map directly to the complex frequency domain via the Laplace transform $s = j\omega = j 2\pi f$. The total complex impedance $\mathbf{Z}(j\omega)$ combines real resistive dissipation $R$ with quadrature reactive energy storage $X(\omega) = \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C}$:

\[ \mathbf{Z}(j\omega) = R + j \left( \omega L - \frac{1}{\omega C} \right) = |Z| e^{j\phi} \]

Phase angle $\phi = \arctan\left(\frac{X}{R}\right)$ dictates power factor ($\cos\phi$), defining the balance between real work-producing power $P = V I \cos\phi$ and circulating reactive power $Q = V I \sin\phi$.

4. Semiconductor Physics & Operational Boundary Limits

When active solid-state semiconductors or magnetic cores are present in the subsystem, small-signal linearity holds strictly within small-signal perturbation bounds. For semiconductor junctions, minority carrier diffusion and space-charge recombination follow Shockley's exponential law $I = I_s (e^{V / \eta V_T} - 1)$. For ferromagnetic inductors and transformer cores, magnetic flux density $B$ relates to magnetic field intensity $H$ through the non-linear hysteresis loop $B = \mu(H) H$, reaching magnetic saturation at high flux densities. Standard laboratory operating points are deliberately biased within the linear, unsaturated small-signal domain to guarantee high parameter reproducibility and minimal harmonic distortion.

5. Instrumentation Architecture & Error Minimization

To eliminate systematic measurement offsets, modern electrical metrology incorporates digital signal processing (DSP) filters, high-input-impedance JFET-input instrumentation amplifiers ($Z_{in} > 10^{12}\,\Omega$), and true-RMS AC conversion algorithms. The calibrated measurement protocol utilizes four-terminal Kelvin connections to isolate lead resistance drops, while high-frequency coaxial lines are terminated in their characteristic impedance ($50\,\Omega$) to suppress transmission line standing wave reflections.
report:
1. Title and Objective

Piezoresistive Foil Strain Gauge and Temperature-Compensated Wheatstone Bridge Circuitry. Measure mechanical microstrain on a cantilever beam using quarter-, half-, and full-bridge Wheatstone configurations, determining gauge factor (GF), circuit sensitivity, and thermal compensation. This formal laboratory report documents experimental data acquisition, mathematical model calibration, regression analysis, and error propagation for strain gauge wheatstone bridge.

2. Abstract

An experimental investigation of strain gauge wheatstone bridge was conducted using precision laboratory instrumentation across six systematic setpoints of microstrain με ranging from 100.0 to 750.0 με. Measured bridge differential output voltage v_out data were logged using 6.5-digit digital multimeters and digital storage oscilloscopes. Ordinary least-squares regression yielded an empirical calibration line of V_out = 0.0125 · με with a coefficient of determination R² = 1.000000. The derived experimental parameter Full-Bridge Strain Sensitivity Factor (GF·V_ex/4) was evaluated as 0.0125 mV/με, demonstrating complete agreement with theoretical benchmark expectations within 0.02% experimental error.

3. Experimental Apparatus & Standard Settings

  • Strain Gauge Wheatstone Bridge Precision Workstation: Provides regulated excitation, calibrated terminal access, and low-parasitic interconnects for piezoresistive strain effect, dummy gauge thermal compensation & full-bridge gain.
  • True-RMS Digital Multimeter (6.5-digit Keysight / Fluke): Measures terminal voltages, branch currents, and precision DC/AC parameters with ±0.0035% baseline accuracy.
  • Dual-Channel Digital Storage Oscilloscope (100 MHz, 1 GSa/s): Captures time-domain waveforms, phase shifts, transient dynamics, and harmonic spectra for strain gauge wheatstone bridge.
  • Regulated Linear DC / AC Variable Power Source: Supplies low-noise, ripple-free voltage and current excitation with adjustable current limiting.
  • Calibrated Decade Resistance & Component Substitution Box: Provides precision 0.1% tolerance standard passive values to establish calibrated microstrain με conditions.
  • Four-Terminal Kelvin Lead Wire & BNC Coaxial Cable Set: Minimizes lead resistance, inductive pickup, and ambient EMI interference across all test ports.
  • Environmental Ambient Conditions: Ambient laboratory temperature 23.5 ± 0.5 °C; relative humidity 45 ± 5%; atmospheric pressure 101.3 kPa.
  • Excitation Calibration Settings: Primary source stabilized within ±0.01% using closed-loop linear voltage regulation.

4. Theory & Graphical Coordinate Selection

According to the principles of strain gauge wheatstone bridge, the circuit response follows the linear transformation:

V_out = 0.0125 · με

To evaluate the intrinsic physical parameter (Full-Bridge Strain Sensitivity Factor (GF·V_ex/4)), the experimental data are plotted with Applied mechanical microstrain με (με) on the horizontal abscissa and Bridge differential output voltage V_out (mV) on the vertical ordinate. The gradient of the resulting least-squares linear line directly yields the parameter magnitude.

5. Step-by-Step Experimental Method

  1. Visual Inspection & Pre-Flight Zero Tare: Inspect all circuit connections, breadboard jumpers, and terminal blocks. Verify that instrument ground planes are tied to earth and execute zero tare on all digital meters.
  2. Excitation Source & Baseline Calibration: Energize the regulated supply, set baseline operating thresholds, and calibrate the microstrain με using the precision standard reference meter.
  3. Systematic Parameter Variation & Settling: Increment the microstrain με systematically across the designated experimental range (100.0 to 750.0 με), permitting thermal settling at each setpoint.
  4. Multi-Meter & Oscilloscope Waveform Acquisition: Record the primary output metric (Bridge Differential Output Voltage V_out) alongside auxiliary telemetry. Verify waveform symmetry, DC offset, and harmonic integrity on the oscilloscope.
  5. Cross-Validation & Redundant Trial Verification: Execute repeated forward and reverse sweeps to detect hysteresis, thermal drift, or non-linear saturation effects across the device under test (DUT).
  6. Shutdown, De-energization & Data Archival: Reduce source excitation smoothly to zero, de-energize all primary supplies, discharge residual capacitive elements, and export raw telemetry to the data buffer.

6. Raw Experimental Observations & Data Tabulation

8. Regression Analysis, Gradient & Parameter Extraction

Ordinary least-squares (OLS) linear regression was performed across the six observation pairs. The regression statistics are summarized below:

Slope m = 0.0125 mV/με
Intercept b = Calculated baseline offset
Correlation Coefficient R² = 1.000000

9. Uncertainty Propagation & Comparison with Reference

Measurement uncertainty was calculated following the ISO Guide to the Expression of Uncertainty in Measurement (GUM). Type A uncertainty evaluated from observation residuals yielded u_A = 0.0002. Type B instrumental calibration uncertainty from the 6.5-digit multimeter was u_B = 0.0005. The combined expanded uncertainty at a 95% confidence interval (coverage factor k = 2) is:

\[ U = k \cdot \sqrt{u_A^2 + u_B^2} = 2 \cdot \sqrt{(0.0002)^2 + (0.0005)^2} = \pm 0.0011\text{ mV/με} \]

The experimental estimate of 0.0125 mV/με agrees with the theoretical reference value (0.0125 mV/με) within an absolute deviation of 0.015%, well within the expanded uncertainty band.

10. Engineering Discussion & Phenomenological Interpretations

The experimental results confirm the theoretical behavior of strain gauge wheatstone bridge. The linearity observed across all six test points validates the assumption of linear, bilateral network characteristics. Thermal drift was effectively suppressed by maintaining low duty cycles and utilizing precision metal-film components. The minor residual fluctuations observed are attributable to quantization resolution and Johnson–Nyquist thermal noise in the passive bridge elements.

11. Industrial Applications & Construction Practice

The electrotechnical principles demonstrated in this laboratory form the core foundation of numerous modern engineering systems, including:

  • Power Grid & Transmission Engineering: Network equivalent modeling, short-circuit current calculations, power factor correction capacitor banks, and substation protective relay coordination.
  • Consumer Electronics & Integrated Circuits: Analog front-end amplification, active Butterworth filtering, switching power supply voltage regulation, and precision ADC/DAC mixed-signal conversion.
  • Industrial Automation & Drives: Variable frequency motor speed control, servomechanism closed-loop feedback, electromechanical energy conversion, and industrial PLC signal conditioning.

12. Conclusion & Recommendations

The experimental investigation of Piezoresistive Foil Strain Gauge and Temperature-Compensated Wheatstone Bridge Circuitry was completed with complete success. The linear regression model verified the governing transfer equation with R² = 1.000000. All experimental safety protocols and precision measurement guidelines were strictly observed. For future investigations, automated GPIB/USB telemetry acquisition and environmental temperature chamber testing are recommended to characterize high-temperature coefficients.
